Tutorial Component 
The tutorial component is held every week and is designed to support students in 
developing strong conceptual understanding, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills 
in physics. 
Tutorials provide a structured and supportive environment in which students actively 
engage with physics problems related to the course material. Each session focuses on 
reasoning, application, and analysis, rather than passive review. 
During tutorials, we work through carefully selected problems together. Students receive 
real-time guidance and feedback, encouraging them to: 
• Think critically about physical situations in a variety of contexts 
• Apply physics concepts with increasing confidence 
• Refine the accuracy, clarity, and coherence of the reasoning 
This iterative, hands-on problem-solving process strengthens conceptual foundations and 
cultivates a methodical scientific mindset—skills essential for success in both academic 
studies and professional scientific or technical fields.

To ensure productive and focused tutorial sessions, students are expected to come 
prepared. Please bring the following to every tutorial, starting with the first one:

Description 
The laboratory component of this course provides students with hands-on experience in 
mechanics. Through structured experimental investigations, students develop a deeper 
understanding of physical principles while strengthening experimental technique, data 
analysis, uncertainty evaluation, and scientific communication skills. 
 
 
Learning Outcomes 
By the end of the lab sequence, students will be able to: 
• Set up and conduct experiments in mechanics. 
• Collaborate effectively in small groups during investigations. 
• Measure and report precision of analog and digital instruments. 
• Identify and distinguish between systematic and random errors. 
• Estimate, calculate, and interpret uncertainties in measurements and final results. 
• Assess whether results agree within uncertainties. 
 
Lab Format 
• Students will work in groups of two or three. 
• Preparation is essential: read the lab manual and textbook sections and complete 
any assigned pre-lab tasks before arriving.

3 Theory and Procedure
1 Purpose
In this lab we will begin to build the foundation for working withmeasurement
uncertainty. Before learning formal methods, it is essential to practice concepts
such asestimation,bounding, andorder-of-magnitude reasoning. Especially when it is
useful in situations where quantities cannot be measured directly. These skills help us

3.5.2 Illustration of Order of Magnitude Calculation
Any time you use anestimatedquantity in a calculation, you are performing anorder
of magnitude (OM) calculation. The purpose is not to obtain an exact answer,
but to check whether the result falls in a reasonable range.
Theorder of magnitudeof a quantity refers to the power of ten that best describes it.
For example:
• The height of a typical building might be written as∼ 101 metres (tens of
metres).
•The length of an entire campus might be∼102 metres (hundreds of metres).
Thus, saying that the length of the Science Building is
•“about 100 metres,” or
•“between 50 and 200 metres,”
are both acceptable order-of-magnitude estimates. What matters is that the result
lands in the correctballpark.
3.5.3 When are Order of Magnitude Calculations used?
Order of magnitude reasoning is common in science and engineering:
• Before experiments:to anticipate what range of values to expect, and to
decide which instruments or methods are suitable.
• During data collection:to check whether preliminary results make sense in
real time.
• Afterward:to identify errors, such as unit mistakes, which often shift results
by entire orders of magnitude.

A.1 Significant Figures (SigFigs)
Why they matter.Significant figures reflect the precision of a measurement and
keep reported results consistent with the quality of the data.
Core rules
•All nonzero digits are significant (e.g., 123.4 has 4 sig figs).
•Zeros between nonzero digits are significant (e.g., 1002 has 4 sig figs).
•Leading zeros arenotsignificant (e.g., 0.00450 has 3 sig figs).
• Trailing zeros are significantifa decimal point is present (e.g., 45.00 has 4 sig
figs; 4500 has 2 sig figs unless written as4.500×103).
Operations
• Multiplication/Division:keep the same number of sig figs as the factor with
the fewest sig figs.
Example:(2.6cm)×(3.14cm) = 8.164cm 2→8.16cm 2 (3 sig figs).
•Addition/Subtraction:round to the least precisedecimal place.
Example:12.30 + 0.456 = 12.756→12.76(hundredths place).

figs for each edge, keep 3 sig figs. Match this to your instrument’s markings.)
